items.item: The hook's 'quick fix' framing matters: a learner who thinks the bypass is rare or exotic will underweight it; it is the single most common real-world misconfiguration behind every one of these five catalogs' own security documentation

items.item: The predict step's point is structural, not procedural — the fix is never 'patch the mask,' because the mask was never broken; the fix is always 'stop handing out bulk credentials'

items.item: The five vendor names are not interchangeable trivia; a learner who can recite all five but can't draw the shared get-metadata/check-permissions/get-credentials/get-data flow from memory has not learned the mechanism, only the vocabulary

items.item: security_invoker on a Postgres view is not a cosmetic detail; omitting it silently runs the view with the owner's privileges, bypassing RLS for the querying user entirely — the exact subtlety this topic's own examples.py caught and fixed while building it

at.step: A row filter and a column mask, both real

items.item: Iceberg REST credential vending being opt-in (a client signals support, a server may decline) means a REST catalog client that never checks storage-credentials can silently fall back to a less-scoped path — worth knowing before assuming every Iceberg REST deployment vends credentials by default

at.step: The open-protocol version has a name too

items.item: Tag-based grants solve a real operational problem (a grant written per-object needs rewriting every time a new object appears) but also widen blast radius silently — a mistagged table inherits every grant on that tag, which is the trade-off worth teaching alongside the convenience

at.step: A grant on a tag survives a table the policy never knew about

items.item: Cross-account sharing and Spark-native fine-grained writes are named rather than reproduced because reproducing them needs a second AWS account or a running Glue job respectively — a learner should not expect a local demo of either and should treat the OUTLINE.md scope note as the actual boundary, not an oversight

The bypass demonstration's power comes from holding the policy, the table and the query identical between the two reads and varying only the credential — a learner who doesn't notice that control is the whole argument will miss why this is proof and not just an assertion
